blurb: Motors, gearing, fluid power, piezo, and artificial muscles — compared on torque density, backdrivability, precision, and cost.
title: Robot Actuators: A Practical Reference
lede: Every robot is a set of compromises made physical, and most of them are made at the actuator: torque density against backdrivability, precision against cost, force against compliance. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} actuator and transmission technologies across seven classes, from brushed DC motors to artificial muscles.

facets.label: Application
facets.tip: Where the technology is mainly used or targeted in robotics — directional, not exhaustive.

facets.label: Density
facets.tip: Directional torque (or force) per unit mass of the complete actuator at robot-relevant duty. Hydraulics anchor the top; ungeared electric motors sit lower than their spec sheets suggest once continuous thermal limits apply.

facets.label: Backdrive
facets.tip: How easily external forces can move the actuator — the proxy for safe contact, force control, and impact tolerance. High gear ratios and lead screws kill it; direct drive, QDD, and fluid muscles preserve it.

facets.label: Precision
facets.tip: Achievable positioning precision in typical use, including transmission backlash and control: Coarse (mm+) · Moderate (0.1–1 mm) · Fine (µm–0.1 mm) · Sub-micron.

facets.label: Cost
facets.tip: Directional cost per axis at robot-relevant sizes, including drive electronics where inseparable. Volume changes everything — humanoid-scale orders are collapsing prices across the board.
